question_text: In this verse, does the characteristic engage the perceptive faculty — the inner senses (hearing, sight, taste, touch, smell) and spiritual discernment — and if so, which inner sense and how? Record none if it does not.

distinct_answers.text: The perceptive faculty is engaged at the point where hatred enters the inner life. Gen 37:4: "when his brothers *saw* that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him" — the perception of favouritism is the trigger. Each new perception (the dream, the words — Gen 37:5, 8) intensifies the hatred. The perception does not merely register facts; it reads relational signals and feeds them to the disposition. In group 550-NEW-02 (righteous hatred): Psa 119:104 — "through your precepts I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way" — perception of truth actively generates hatred of its opposite. Understanding of what is true makes the encounter with falsehood more immediately and viscerally intolerable.

Contempt distorts perception in a specific way: it causes the person to see the despised object through the lens of the low-worth verdict already rendered. Once Esau has despised the birthright, he cannot perceive it accurately — its value is invisible to him. Psa 10:3: the wicked "curses and renounces the Lord" — the perception of God has been filtered through a prior verdict of his irrelevance. Contempt is a perception-filter: what is despised becomes imperceptible in its actual worth.

Abhorrence is triggered by perception — the morally repugnant thing must first be seen or encountered. But abhorrence also shapes subsequent perception: once something is abhorred, it becomes perceived as repugnant in all future encounters. Group 247-001 (she.qets): Eze 8:10 — the prophet is brought to see the detestable things engraved on the wall — the vision makes visible what has been provoking divine abhorrence. In the inverted form (group 252-002): those who abhor justice (Amo 5:10) perceive the truth-speaker as the repugnant thing — their perceptive faculty has been reorganised around the inverted abhorrence.

Cruelty impairs the perceptive faculty in a specific direction: it prevents the person from registering the suffering of others as a claim on their conduct. Pro 12:10: "the righteous has regard for the life of his beast" — the righteous person perceives animal life as worthy of regard; the wicked person does not perceive it in this way. The cruel person's perception has been reorganised so that what should trigger mercy and restraint does not register as such.

Reproach restructures perception. Psa 22:6: "I am a worm and not a man" — the person perceives themselves through the lens of others' contempt. Isa 51:7: "fear not the reproach of man" — the command implies that reproach has reorganised the person's perception of threat, making every potential reproach-encounter something to be feared. The characteristic shapes how the person perceives themselves, others' regard, and the social environment.

1Pe 5:8: "be watchful" — the adversary relationship requires heightened perceptive alertness. The adversary who prowls must be perceived accurately and in time. The characteristic sharpens the perceptive faculty toward vigilant awareness of threat.

Malice presupposes the perception of another's suffering and then evaluates that suffering as a positive good. Eze 25:6 — the nations see the land of Israel devastated and clap their hands. The perceptive faculty has been reorganised by malice so that the perception of another's destruction triggers pleasure rather than compassion.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** Yes — God's righteousness is heard: "the Spirit convicts the world concerning righteousness" (Joh 16:8, VSG M26-A1-005), and proclamation of it is made to be heard and received (Psa 35:28; 71:24; 145:7). Encountering God's righteousness produces an inner perception — Felix "heard" the reasoning about righteousness and self-control and was alarmed (Act 24:25, VSG M26-A1-006). The perception here is cognitive-auditory: the standard of divine righteousness is received through hearing and registered internally.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Yes — hunger and thirst for righteousness (Mat 5:6, VSG M26-A2-006) names a perceptual-desire orientation: the person is constituted to perceive righteousness as desirable, to sense its absence as a lack. This is the spiritual-perceptual analog of physical hunger — an inner sense that registers the absence of what is needed. Uprightness enables recognition of right paths (Pro 2:9, VSG 1212-002) — a discernment function that is inherently perceptive.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Yes — uprightness enables a specific perceptive capacity: "then you will understand righteousness and justice and equity, every good path" (Pro 2:9, VSG 1212-002). The upright person perceives what is right — they see what others miss. Isa 30:10 (VSG 1214-001) names the refusal of this perception: "do not see," "prophesy to us smooth things" — the demand that the prophets not perceive and report what is right. Uprightness is in part a perceptive virtue — the capacity to see truly.
**[C — Justification]** Justification as an act does not primarily engage the perceptive faculty. The act is declarative and received by faith, not by perception. Silence.

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Yes — the cry for justice (Luk 18:3, VSG 944-001) presupposes perception of injustice: the widow perceives that she has been wronged and appeals on the basis of that perception. The capacity to perceive that wrong has occurred is the precondition for the cry for justice. D's perceptive engagement is the moral recognition of injustice.

**[E — Condemnation]** Yes — self-condemnation (autokatakritos, Tit 3:11) presupposes self-perception: the person perceives their own conduct and finds it condemnable. The condemning conscience operates by perceiving moral failure in the self. The Ninevites perceiving the greatness of the one before them (Mat 12:41, VSG 4846-001) — their repentance arose from spiritual perception.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Yes — the reckoning faculty engages perception in a specific mode: the faculty considers (logizomai), weighs, and deliberates — all of which require perceiving the things being compared. "Count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God" (Rom 6:11) requires perceiving one's own status accurately. "The sufferings of this present time" (Rom 8:18) must be perceived before they can be weighed. The reckoning faculty is a form of organized inner perception applied to moral reality.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Yes — but inverted. "They do not know how to do right" (Amo 3:10, VSG 1214-001) names the failure of moral perception in the wicked. "None of the wicked shall understand" (Dan 12:10, VSG 1225-001). Wickedness impairs the perceptive faculty for righteousness — the wicked person in the land of uprightness "does not see the majesty of the Lord" (Isa 26:10, VSG 5617-001).

**[CLUSTER — T3.1]** E. The perceptive faculty is engaged across the cluster in specific modes: (1) auditory perception of the proclaimed standard (A1); (2) hunger-perception of righteousness as desirable (A2); (3) discernment-perception of right paths (B); (4) perception of injustice as the trigger for the cry for justice (D); (5) self-perception as the ground of self-condemnation (E); (6) organized deliberative perception as the mode of moral reckoning (F). Wickedness impairs all these perceptive modes (G).

VCG08 (Pro 6:6 pronoia): observation as the basis for purposive foresight. M15-E engages perception primarily as input to planning, not as its core function.

VCG04 (Dan 7:28 se.khal): focused contemplative attention on received content. VCG02 (Matt 1:20 enthumeomai): reflective perception of a complex situation. M15-F is second-order perception — dwelling on what has already been perceived.
VCG01 (2Cor 4:4 noēma): blinding targets thought-content (the output of perception), not the perceptive act. M15-G is the content produced by perception, not the perceptive activity.

VCG01 (1Cor 1:18): the logos reveals the state of the hearer's inner perceptive capacity — the same word is perceived as folly or power depending on inner state. M15-H is a diagnostic of perception, not itself perception.
Jude 9 (dialegō): reasoned disputation engages deliberative cognition applied to contended claims. Perceptive engagement is thin in BOUNDARY's single active verse.

Yes — distazō is engaged by perception: Peter sees the wind and waves (Mat 14:30) — perceptual awareness of threat triggers the doubt. Mat 28:17 — they see Jesus and some doubt; the doubt arises from the act of seeing and failing to complete the perceptual-to-trust movement. Doubt in distazō is specifically post-perceptual — it arises after seeing, not before.

Yes — two perceptive senses are evidenced: (1) Sight: ra.tsah group 795-002 (Isa 42:1): "my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice" — God's inner sight and discernment directed at the Servant as the ground of his ra.tsah. Job 33:26 (795-002): the accepted person "sees his face with a shout of joy" — the graced encounter produces a seeing of God's face. (2) Hearing: cha.nan group 984-001 (Psa 4:1): "answer me when I call... hear my prayer" — grace is sought through the hearing of God; the grace-cry is addressed to the divine ear. Psa 27:7: "hear, O Lord, when I cry aloud; be gracious to me and answer me" — hearing and grace are paired explicitly.

Yes — sight. Jer 1:12 (632-002): "you have seen well" — ya.tav applied to the prophetic perceptive act; accurate seeing is named as a form of goodness. The good perception of the prophet coheres with the divine standard of what is genuinely right.

M46-A's most central finding is the impairment of the perceptive faculty. Isa 6:10 names it directly: make the heart fat so they cannot see (eyes), cannot hear (ears), cannot understand (heart), and cannot turn. Inner closure systematically closes down inner and outer perception. Rev 3:17 names the outcome: "not realising" (ouk oidas) — the perceptual blindness of the self-assessed wealthy person who cannot perceive their actual inner condition. Job 12:5 adds: "in the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune" — the at-ease person cannot perceive the reality of suffering as genuine.

Insatiability engages perception in its distorted form: "eyes never satisfied with riches" (Ecc 4:8 — enayim lo tis.bah). The eyes are engaged but never reach the point of having seen enough — the perceptual organ of desire (the eye as the organ of wanting) is functioning but cannot close. The deceitfulness of riches (apatē, Mat 13:22) also engages perception: riches deceive, which requires the perceptual faculty to be deceived — the person sees riches but sees them incorrectly.
M46-C does not explicitly engage the perceptive faculty. The wisdom tradition operates through the understanding and evaluative faculties (T3.2) rather than through perception directly.

M46-D engages perception in the forward-looking mode: Moses "was looking to the reward" (Heb 11:26 — apoblepō, to look away toward something) — his perception was re-oriented from Egypt's visible treasures to the invisible future reward. The revaluation that characterises M46-D requires a redirected perceptive faculty — seeing what is truly valuable as opposed to what is visibly valuable.

M01-A engages the perceptive faculty primarily through **sight** and **hearing** as triggers of reverential awe. Exo 14:31 (Israel witnessed God's power over Egypt and feared the Lord — sight of divine action triggers reverential fear); Psa 145:6 (God's deeds produce fear-inducing wonder in those who "speak of them" — verbal-cognitive perception); Hag 1:12 (hearing the prophetic word produces fear — auditory trigger). Also spiritual discernment: Job 1:1 (Job's fear of God is the inner moral quality that discerns rightly across all circumstances — a discernment-based orientation rather than a perception-based response).

M01-B engages the perceptive faculty extensively, primarily through **sight**: 1Sa 17:24 (sight of Goliath produces extreme fear), Mat 14:26 (sight of Jesus walking on water triggers fear), Dan 5:6 (sight of the writing on the wall produces dismay/fear), Luk 2:9 (sight of the angel and divine glory fills the shepherds with fear). **Hearing** also triggers B-fear: 2Ki 19:6 (fear triggered by Assyrian threatening words), Jer 51:46 (fearfulness from successive alarming reports). Spiritual discernment: 1Sa 18:12 (Saul's fear of David "rooted in theological perception — he recognises that God's presence has transferred from himself to David").

M01-C engages **sight** as the primary perceptive trigger: Dan 2:31 (the great image's appearance produces fear), Job 41:14 (Leviathan's face radiates terror outward — sight of Leviathan produces terror in beholders). Also the inner sense of **hearing**: Jer 20:10 (Jeremiah hears whispers of "terror on every side" — auditory trigger for the encircling-terror experience).

M01-D engages **sight** and **hearing**: Isa 21:3 (the vision the prophet sees produces dismay so overwhelming he cannot see), Dan 7:7 (the fearful beast — its appearance produces fear as the immediate inner response to sight of its dreadful strength). The distortion of sight and hearing (cannot see, speechlessness) is the distinctive pattern of D's perceptive engagement.

M01-E engages **hearing** as a primary perceptive trigger: Exo 19:16 (thunder and trumpet at Sinai produced involuntary trembling — the auditory trigger is explicit). Amos 3:6 (a trumpet blast naturally produces trembling — auditory). Job 37:1 ("Elihu's heart trembles and leaps at the **thunder** of God's voice" — auditory trigger for somatic trembling). Also sight: Eze 26:16 (trembling seizes the sea-princes at **witnessing** Tyre's fall — visual trigger for somatic trembling).

M01-F engages **hearing** as a primary trigger: Jer 49:23 (anxiety seizes Damascus "on hearing bad news"); 2Cor 12:20 (Paul's anticipatory dread rooted in "thought about what he may find" — imaginative rather than actual perceptive engagement). Also **sight**: Deu 28:67 ("dread explicitly located in the heart and tied to what **the eyes see**" — visual experience driving anticipatory dread).

M01-G timidity's perceptive triggers are not explicitly described in the verse evidence. The threat situations (storm, master's harshness, persecution) are implied but the specific inner-sense engagement is not named.

The perceptive faculty is engaged across all sub-groups of M01. The dominant inner senses are **sight** (primary across B, C, D, E-VCG-03, A) and **hearing** (primary in A, E-VCG-01, F). Spiritual discernment is evidenced in M01-A (Job 1:1) and M01-B (1Sa 18:12). The perceptive faculty is the trigger-gateway for fear across the cluster — what is seen or heard initiates the fear-state. This confirms that M01 is heavily perception-driven: the characteristic is routinely initiated by perceptive engagement with external reality.

Yes. Act 17:16 (M02-D-VCG-03) is the definitive evidence: Paul's spirit is provoked by sight — he sees Athens filled with idols, and this visual moral perception ignites the inner provocation. The inner sense engaged is moral-spiritual sight: the perceptive faculty reads the moral significance of what is observed (idol-worship = violation of God's exclusive claim) and the anger is the response to that reading. The inner sense is not merely physical seeing but moral discernment of what is seen.

Neh 5:6 (M02-B-VCG-04): Nehemiah hears the outcry of the oppressed poor and becomes very angry — the inner sense of hearing is the channel through which righteous anger is aroused. The perceptive faculty receives the moral cry and anger responds.

God's anger in M02-B-VCG-01 is consistently aroused by perception of Israel's acts: Num 25:3 (kindled by Baal worship), Jos 7:1 (kindled by one man's covenant breach) — the divine perceptive faculty registers the moral violation and the anger is the responsive state.

Yes. Several perceptive faculties are engaged. Sight: Elisha's weeping follows a fixed, penetrating gaze — the prophetic vision of coming catastrophe produces grief (2Ki 8:11 — M03-A-VCG-04). Jesus's grief in Mar 3:5 follows perceiving the Pharisees' hardness of heart — grief arising from spiritual discernment of moral stubbornness. Conscience as inner moral perception: God marks those whose sighing evidences genuine inward grief over witnessed wickedness (Eze 9:4 — M03-E-VCG-01) — conscience-driven perception of sin producing grief. Taste: bitterness in M03-G is explicitly a taste metaphor — the scroll bitter in the stomach (Rev 10:9-10 — M03-G-VCG-01), life made bitter (Gen 26:35 — M03-G-VCG-01). Hearing: God hears the sound of weeping (Psa 6:8 — M03-A-VCG-04); groaning is heard by others (Lam 1:21 — M03-E-VCG-01).

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Exultation is consistently triggered by perception — hearing (Exo 18:9 — Jethro heard of God's acts), seeing (Dan 6:23 — the king sees Daniel unharmed; Isa 66:14 — "you shall see, and your heart shall rejoice"), and the inner perception of divine reality (Psa 13:5 — trust in steadfast love as the ground of the heart's rejoicing). The evidence shows exultation engaging primarily inner hearing and inner sight — the capacity to perceive God's acts and character as true and real.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, consistently. The evidence shows Joy arising from perception across all inner senses: (1) **Sight** — "When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly" (Mat 2:10); "when she has found it" (Luk 15:9); "the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord" (Joh 20:20); Psa 97:8 ("Zion hears and is glad"); Isa 66:14 ("you shall see, and your heart shall rejoice"); (2) **Hearing** — Neh 8:12 (joy from understanding what was declared); Psa 34:2 ("let the humble hear and be glad"); "recognizing Peter's voice" (Act 12:14); (3) **Taste** — Ecc 9:7 ("eat your bread with joy") — taste-mediated festive joy; (4) **Spiritual discernment** — Act 11:23 (Barnabas "saw the grace of God, he was glad") — spiritual perception of divine grace producing joy. Perception is the most common immediate trigger for Joy in the corpus.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes, but distinctively. Suffering-Joy is characterised by perception of what is not (yet) visible: 1Pe 1:8 ("though you do not now see him, you believe in him") — the rejoicing arises despite the absence of visible evidence; Joh 8:56 (Abraham "saw" Christ's day through faith-vision, not physical sight) — inner spiritual perception of future reality. Luk 1:44 (adjacent — "the baby in my womb leaped for joy" at the sound of Mary's greeting) — the most physicality-affirming perception-instance: hearing as the trigger of the most bodily form of rejoicing. M04-F: Psa 39:13 ("that I may smile again before I depart") — the perceptive capacity is directed toward the self and its diminishing life; ba.lag is triggered by mortality-perception.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. Gladness is consistently perception-triggered: Gen 1:4–31 — God "saw" (ra'ah) that it was good — the perceptive act produces the evaluative declaration; Gen 40:16 — the baker "saw that the interpretation was favorable" — visual/perceptive recognition initiating inner brightening; 2Sa 18:27 — David identifies the runner perceptually and judges him "a good man"; Psa 97:11 (M04-B adjacent, but the pattern) — "light is sown for the righteous"; M04-O-VCG-01: hearing good news (Pro 15:30; Isa 52:7) — the auditory perceptive faculty is the trigger.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, in several registers: (1) **Hearing** — the primary perceptive trigger for law-delight: Psa 119:16 ("I will delight in your statutes") — statutes heard and received; Jer 6:10 ("the word of the Lord is to them an object of scorn; they take no pleasure in it") — the blocked ear blocking Delight; (2) **Taste/eating** — Isa 55:2 ("eat what is good, and delight yourselves in rich food" — a.nog) — the gustatory metaphor for Delight's perceptive dimension; (3) **Smell** — ni.cho.ach aroma — the olfactory sense as the medium through which correct worship is perceived as pleasing; (4) **Sight** — Rev 13:3; 17:8 (the whole earth marveling at the beast's apparent resurrection) — visual perception triggering the captivation of corrupt Delight; (5) **Inner perception** — Psa 51:6 ("you delight in truth in the inward being") — God's perceptive regard penetrating to the inner being's truthfulness.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes — more explicitly than any other M04 characteristic: (1) **Sight** — Psa 27:4 ("to gaze upon the beauty of the Lord"); (2) **Smell** — Gen 8:21 ("when the Lord smelled the pleasing aroma"); the entire ni.cho.ach corpus is olfactory-mediated; (3) **Taste** — Psa 34:8 ("taste and see that the Lord is good" — cross-assigned to M04-K); (4) **Hearing** — Pro 16:24 (gracious words received auditorily); (5) **Touch** — Deu 28:54, 56 (the delicate woman who would not set her foot on the ground — touch-sensitivity as the somatic marker of pampered Pleasure).

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes — more explicitly than any other M04 characteristic in the visual-perceptive mode: (1) **"Marvellous in our eyes"** (Psa 118:23) — sight as the perceptive organ of Wonder; (2) **"Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things"** (Psa 119:18) — petition for perceptive opening; (3) **"They saw the deeds of the Lord, his wondrous works in the deep"** (Psa 107:24) — Wonder grounded in direct visual perceptive encounter; (4) **"Stop and consider the wondrous works of God"** (Job 37:14) — the imperative to attend perceptively; (5) **"Manoah and his wife were watching"** (Judg 13:19) — wonder-producing encounter witnessed perceptively; (6) **Mar 1:27** (thambeō at teaching heard and seen); **Mar 10:32** (seeing Jesus walk ahead in determination).

**[CLUSTER]** E — Perceptive faculty engagement is evidenced across all seven, but with distinctive profiles: (1) **Most visually-perceptive**: Wonder (Char 6) — "marvellous in our eyes" (Psa 118:23); "open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things" (Psa 119:18); Pleasure (Char 5) — "gaze upon the beauty of the Lord" (Psa 27:4); (2) **Most hearing-perceptive**: Gladness (Char 3) — "good news refreshes the bones" (Pro 15:30); Pro 12:25 (word making glad); Joy (Char 2) — Neh 8:12 (comprehension producing Joy); (3) **Most olfactory-perceptive**: Pleasure (Char 5) — the entire ni.cho.ach aroma corpus (38 verses); (4) **Spiritual/faith-perceptive**: Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — 1Pe 1:8 ("though you do not now see him, you believe") — perception of what is not visible; (5) **Inner-cognitive perceptive**: Gladness (Char 3) — the evaluative act of perceiving what is good; Wonder (Char 6) — perceiving what exceeds categories. The cluster as a whole is deeply perception-engaged, confirming that M04's positive inner states are not internally-generated emotions but responses to genuinely perceived realities. The cluster's perceptive richness spans all five sensory modes plus the inner perceptive faculties.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Sight and hearing are prominent in the shame-triggering sequences. Ezr 8:22 (vc=65494) — Ezra's anticipatory shame arises from having publicly declared God's sufficiency (his own words, heard by the king); asking for soldiers would expose the inconsistency. The shame is perceptively triggered by the anticipated gap between what has been seen and what would be seen. Psa 34:5 (vc=37340) — "those who look to him are radiant" — the direction of the perceptive faculty (toward God) determines whether shame falls. The seared-conscience passages show shame's absence being linked to failed perception: "they do not see" God's lifted hand (Isa 26:11, vc=65534). The shame of idol-worship (M07-B-VCG-02) is triggered by seeing the idols' worthlessness exposed — a perceptive event (the idol fails to act) produces the inner shame collapse.

**[CHAR-2]** E — CHAR-2 primarily impairs perception by collapsing the upward gaze: the humiliated are "dismayed and confounded." The haughty eyes targeted in Isa 5:15 and Psa 18:27 show the perceptive faculty as the site of prideful distortion. In the VCG-03 divine-abasement mode, CHAR-2 can be read as perception-correcting: the proud are forced to see what they actually are.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Perception is engaged in CHAR-5 through the contempt-er's misperception of worth (they do not see the genuine worth of the person they despise) and through the recipient's perception of their own contempt-received condition. Psa 14:6 — "shame the plans of the poor" — shows how contempt targets the poor person's inner plans and confidence (their hopeful perception of their own possibilities). CHAR-5 impairs the recipient's hopeful perception by forcing them to see themselves through the contempt-er's false worth-assessment.

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 enables moral perception: the person with a clean conscience and blameless hands can perceive their own moral condition accurately (they know they are innocent) and can perceive God's response accurately (God confirms the innocent's claim, Gen 20:6). The loss of CHAR-6 impairs moral perception: Psa 73:13's crisis is a perceptive failure — the psalmist cannot perceive why innocent suffering exists; Hos 8:5's incapacity-for-innocence is a state in which the people cannot perceive their own moral condition accurately because it has been so long distorted by idolatry.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's perceptual engagement reveals a consistent bidirectional pattern: shame impairs horizontal perception (the humiliated cannot see their situation clearly; the contempt-shamed person cannot see their own worth accurately) while corrective shame can deepen vertical perception (Char 1 M07-C — shame before God enabling the person to see what God requires; Char 5 — divine reversal correcting the world's perceptual distortions). Every form of shame involves a distorted perception that needs correction. Haughty eyes (Char 2 — Isa 5:15; Psa 18:27) are the perceptive faculty's pride-distorted form; the seared conscience (Chars 1, 4) is the perceptive faculty's moral-distorted form; contempt (Char 5) is the perceptive faculty's worth-distorted form. The cluster's positive pole (Char 6) represents the perceptive faculty in its undistorted form — seeing one's moral condition accurately enough to claim innocence before God.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. CHAR-1 engages the perceptive faculty primarily through the inner sense of spiritual sight — the capacity to perceive God, divine majesty, and divine judgment. Two verses name the perceptive closure directly: Psa 10:4 (vc=34074, M08-A2-VCG-02) — "the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'there is no God'" — CHAR-1 closes the perceptive faculty for God so completely that seeking God does not occur and God is declared absent from the inner horizon; Isa 26:10 (vc=34024, M08-A4-VCG-05) — "the wicked person's inner perceptual faculty is closed to the Lord's majesty even in a land of uprightness; their corruption prevents them from seeing the greatness that should prompt reverence." CHAR-1 also closes perception of divine judgment: Psa 10:5 (vc=34166, M08-A4-VCG-03) — "God's judgments are on high — at a height that the arrogant wicked cannot perceive or reach, so his pride blinds him to the divine standard that will ultimately judge him."
